question.worked_solution:
The multiplicative property of modular congruences states that if

$$
a≡b\,\text{and}\,c≡d\,(\text{mod}\,n),
$$

then, we have 

$$
ac≡bd\,(\text{mod}\,n).
$$

First, we decompose the exponent into a product of smaller exponents. For example,

$$
{36}^{4}=(9\cdot 4)^{4}={9}^{2}\cdot {9}^{2}\cdot {4}^{2}\cdot {4}^{2}.
$$

Next, we note the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{9}^{2} & ≡81\, & (\text{mod}\,11) \\  & ≡7\cdot 11+4\, & (\text{mod}\,11) \\  & ≡7\cdot 0+4\, & (\text{mod}\,11) \\  & ≡4\, & (\text{mod}\,11) \\ {4}^{2} & ≡16\, & (\text{mod}\,11) \\  & ≡1\cdot 11+5\, & (\text{mod}\,11) \\  & ≡1\cdot 0+5\, & (\text{mod}\,11) \\  & ≡5\, & (\text{mod}\,11)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by the multiplicative property of congruences, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{36}^{4} & ≡{9}^{2}\cdot {9}^{2}\cdot {4}^{2}\cdot {4}^{2}\, & (\text{mod}\,11) \\  & ≡4\cdot 4\cdot 5\cdot 5\, & (\text{mod}\,11) \\  & ≡400\, & (\text{mod}\,11) \\  & ≡36\cdot 11+4\, & (\text{mod}\,11) \\  & ≡36\cdot 0+4\, & (\text{mod}\,11) \\  & ≡4\, & (\text{mod}\,11)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
{36}^{4}\text{ mod }11=4.
$$
